Shares of Intel (NASDAQ:INTC) were trading sharply lower on Wednesday, falling as much as 4.6% in early trading and were still down 4.3% as of 1:58 p.m. ET.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

While the overall downturn among chip stocks was a contributing factor, the specific catalyst that sent the semiconductor stock lower was a report of an explosion at Intel's plant in Israel.

Image source: The Motley Fool.

Early reports suggest that three people were seriously injured earlier today in a blast at Intel's manufacturing facility in Kiryat Gat, Israel. In a subsequent press conference, local police and fire officials said they suspected an exploding gas cylinder could have been the catalyst, but the exact cause remains under investigation.

The explosion ignited a fire that has since been extinguished. Firefighters were working to determine the exact circumstances of the blast and were investigating the possibility of a hazardous chemical leak in the wake of the explosion and the resulting blaze.

Local officials said there was no evidence of a terrorist attack and noted that, while the fire was out, security personnel and emergency responders continued to work in the area. The injured parties were evacuated to a nearby hospital and are receiving treatment.

The location is one of Intel's leading facilities in the country, manufacturing "chips that power most of the world's personal computers for over 20 years," according to the company.

As of this writing, it's simply too early to tell if there will be any long-term implications for Intel or its shareholders. Investors should continue to monitor the situation as details emerge and resist the temptation to act before all the facts are available.

title: Is Intel's Record Sales Growth Still Improving?

Is Intel's Record Sales Growth Still Improving?

Image from Pixabay

Intel Corporation (INTC) sold 25.4% more in the three months to June than it did in the same quarter a year earlier. The chipmaker has not grown faster in any quarter of the last ten years. To judge that record properly requires looking at what is normal for the company. So take a guess: in a typical quarter, how much more does Intel sell than a year earlier?

How Unusual Is This For Intel?

The answer is hardly any more. Across the last forty quarters, the median rise in Intel's sales from a year earlier was 1.3%. In a typical quarter, the company sells about what it sold a year before. That makes the quarter to June far outside Intel's normal. Here is the same quarter in each of the last ten years.

The previous high was 24% in the quarter ended March 28, 2020. That period is not shown in the table, but the quarter to June is the first to surpass it and set a brand new record.

What Is Behind Intel's Record Sales Growth?

During a July 23, 2026 call, management said Intel's businesses tied to AI, including data center chips, grew more than 70% from a year earlier. Those businesses now bring in about 70% of Intel's sales. Revenue in Intel's Data Center and Artificial Intelligence unit alone rose 59% from a year earlier. Management also noted that its outlook for server CPU demand had improved again.

Intel also got more for each chip it sold. Management said selling prices rose because Intel sold more of its pricier chips and raised some prices, partly to pass rising costs on to customers.

Is The Latest Quarter Still Improving?

The broader trend reveals more than the June figure on its own. Intel's sales fell 4.1% from a year earlier in the quarter to December 2025. Growth then turned to 7.2% in the quarter to March, before the record in the quarter to June. Intel's growth has now sped up in each of the last two quarters.

One quarter remains a short stretch to measure. Over the last twelve months, Intel's sales grew 7.5% from the twelve months before, which sits well behind the pace of the latest quarter.

When The Record Is Next Tested

In July, management expected sales in the quarter to September to come in about 1.2% above the quarter to June at the midpoint of its forecast range. That quarter has now ended, and Intel has yet to report the results. Management also noted that supply was very tight, with supply growth weighted toward the end of that quarter and into the next, especially for servers. For PCs, management expects PC consumption to fall by a low double-digit percent across 2026.

Intel stock has risen 182.7% over the last twelve months. When the company releases its next quarterly report, the key figure to watch will be sales growth from a year earlier for the quarter to September, tested against June's record.

title: 3 Reasons to Buy Intel Stock Before 2027

3 Reasons to Buy Intel Stock Before 2027
John Ballard, The Motley Fool
Wed, October 14, 2026 at 12:03 PM CDT 5 min read
INTC
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Shares of Intel (NASDAQ: INTC) are up about 180% over the past year, as of Oct. 12, reflecting growing demand for its chips for artificial intelligence (AI) workloads.

The stock is more expensive than it was a year ago, but the prospect of sustainable revenue growth from AI leaves room for further gains over the next several years. "AI is driving unprecedented demand for compute, and as we continue to execute, Intel is well-positioned to capture sustainable growth across our CPU franchise, ASICs, advanced packaging, and vast wafer foundry network," CEO Lip-Bu Tan stated in the 2026 second-quarter earnings report.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Here are three reasons the stock is a buy heading into 2027.

Image source: Intel.
1. Strong execution is producing momentum in financial results

Intel has topped its own financial expectations for seven straight quarters. Beating guidance repeatedly shows the company is executing well against its goals and managing its factories and costs, which can support a higher stock price over time as investors gain confidence. Here are the key highlights from the Q2 earnings report that point to building momentum in the business:

Revenue rose 25% year over year to $16.1 billion -- the company's strongest growth in more than 15 years.

Non-GAAP gross margin (the share of revenue left after production costs) reached 41.8%, more than 12 points higher than a year earlier.

Adjusted earnings per share of $0.42 more than doubled the guidance of $0.20, and reversed a loss of $0.10 in the year-ago quarter.

Higher revenue, better manufacturing yields (more working chips per wafer), and stronger average selling prices drove the strong results, with data-center and AI sales growing 59% to $6.3 billion. AI-related businesses made up roughly 70% of Intel's total revenue in the quarter.

CFO David Zinsner said the near-term goal was to get gross margins "comfortably into the 40s" every quarter -- implying the potential for more gains over its Q2 gross margin. Overall, the prospect of expanding margins is a positive for the stock heading into 2027.

2. AI is driving more demand for Intel's processors than it can supply

AI will need a massive number of central processing units (CPUs), as well as specialized accelerators and graphics processing units (GPUs). CPUs have proven more effective at handling orchestration, data movement, and storage around AI training and inference. The growing use of AI agents (software that performs tasks autonomously) will put more strain on existing compute capacity and is a long-term tailwind for Intel.

Intel faces growing competition in the CPU market from Advanced Micro Devices and Nvidia. But all these companies should continue to post robust growth, since demand for CPUs continues to outrun supply.

AI agents require a four to six times increase in CPU requirements, which is leading to higher core counts and more stable pricing. Beyond servers, Intel sees further opportunities in edge computing and physical AI systems such as industrial equipment and robotics.

These opportunities support analysts' expectations that Intel's revenue will increase by 21% in 2027, reaching $78 billion.

3. Manufacturing progress is opening additional growth opportunities

Intel's foundry efforts (making chips for other companies) and advanced packaging technology, which connects multiple chips into more powerful processing systems, are showing progress. The 18A process is in high-volume production. Better yields and execution in ramping new technologies mean Intel can produce more chips at lower cost, which improves margins and can attract outside customers for Intel's foundry.

Management sees its advanced packaging business potentially reaching billions of dollars in revenue with attractive margins. Revenue is expected to ramp more meaningfully in the second half of 2027 and can also open the door to larger foundry deals.

Intel's foundry posted a Q2 operating loss of $2.1 billion, although the loss narrowed by $348 million over Q1. The foundry's persistent losses have been an overhang on the stock in recent years, but management is working to bring this business to breakeven by the end of 2027 or into 2028. Narrowing losses at Intel Foundry could support a higher stock price in 2027.

Intel's shares are not cheap, trading at a forward price-to-earnings ratio of 67 on 2026 earnings estimates. Even so, accelerating growth, expanding margins, and long-term opportunities in physical AI could still support excellent returns for investors in 2027 and beyond. The forward multiple drops to 49 on 2027 estimates, with analysts expecting 69% annualized earnings growth in the next several years.

title: Applied Materials vs. Intel: Which Technology Stock Is a Better Buy in 2026?
detail:
Applied Materials vs. Intel: Which Technology Stock Is a Better Buy in 2026?
Mike Schwenk, The Motley Fool
Wed, October 14, 2026 at 11:44 AM CDT 10 min read
AMAT
INTC
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

When choosing a technology stock, you can weigh a chipmaker against a supplier of the equipment chipmaking requires. Which is the better buy, Applied Materials (NASDAQ:AMAT) or Intel (NASDAQ:INTC)?

Applied Materials sells the equipment and services that chipmakers use to fabricate semiconductors, and its fiscal year ends in late October. Intel designs and manufactures its own processors for PCs and data centers, and its fiscal year ends in late December. The two companies sit at different points in the semiconductor supply chain.

The case for Applied Materials

In its annual report for the fiscal year ended Oct. 26, 2025, Applied Materials describes itself as the leader in the materials engineering solutions used to produce virtually every semiconductor in the world.

That filing also shows a concentrated customer base, with two customers accounting for about 19% and 15% of net revenue. Customer concentration like this adds risk. In May 2026, Applied announced a new innovation partnership with Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (NYSE:TSM) at its Silicon Valley EPIC Center to develop technologies for AI chips.

On Oct. 6, 2026, Applied also announced a collaboration with Intel, bringing teams together at the EPIC Center and Intel's R&D campus in Hillsboro, Oregon, to work on next-generation transistors and advanced packaging. The announcement gives no financial terms.

In fiscal 2025, revenue reached nearly $28.4 billion, up about 4.4% from the prior year. Net income was close to $7.0 billion, which works out to a net margin of roughly 24.7%, down from 26.4% in fiscal 2024. The dip came from taxes.

Pretax income rose about 14%, but the income tax provision more than doubled to $2.3 billion. The annual report attributes the jump to a $659 million effect from remeasuring deferred tax assets in Singapore and a $407 million valuation allowance on corporate alternative minimum tax credits.

The latest quarter looks stronger than the annual figures. In the quarter ended July 26, 2026, which Applied reported on Aug. 13, revenue rose 25% to $9.1 billion and net income rose 43% to $2.5 billion. The company returned $860 million to shareholders in the quarter through $440 million in share repurchases and $420 million in dividends.

For the fiscal fourth quarter, management guided to revenue of $10.25 billion, plus or minus $500 million.

As of its July 26, 2026 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio, calculated from total debt, was approximately 0.3x, based on total debt of $6.5 billion and shareholders' equity of $25.6 billion.

Hotter-than-expected U.S. inflation raised fears of further interest-rate hikes, pressuring chip stock valuations.

Concerns over increasing competition from Chinese memory chipmakers weighed on the sector.

UBS favors semiconductor and robotics equipment companies and ranks memory stocks lower, citing potential supply increases over the medium term.

The iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) fell more than 4% on Wednesday, putting it on track for its seventh straight losing session, marking its longest losing streak since May 2025.

Hotter-than-expected U.S. inflation and mounting concerns over artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure spending weighed on chip stocks.

See what 10M+ investors are talking about. Get the Stocktwits Daily Rip for what retail is watching right now, free to your inbox

Among SOXX's largest holdings, Advanced Micro Devices (AMD), the fund's most heavily weighted stock, was down over 5% at the time of writing, while Intel (INTC) fell over 3%.

Nvidia (NVDA) and Micron Technology (MU), each accounting for over 7% of the ETF, declined by over 2%.

Chip Stocks Face $1 Trillion Market-Value Wipeout

The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index (SOX) fell over 3.5%. The index has fallen about 10% over six sessions. According to a Bloomberg report, the broader semiconductor sell-off could erase more than $1 trillion in market value.

Among the hardest-hit stocks, Arm Holdings (ARM) plunged nearly 16%, Applied Materials (AMAT) dropped about 14%, and Intel lost 11% over the six-session period.

Broadcom CEO, IMF Warnings Pressure Chip Stocks

Chip stocks came under pressure on Monday after Broadcom (AVGO) CEO Hock Tan warned that access to capital, rather than semiconductor or memory shortages, could become the biggest constraint on AI expansion.

Speaking at a conference in Singapore, Tan also compared some speculative AI investing to casino gambling.

Selling pressure continued on Tuesday as the International Monetary Fund (IMF) warned that weaker-than-expected returns from AI investment could trigger a correction in technology stocks, amplified by rising leverage and concentrated market exposure.

Concerns over increasing competition from Chinese memory chipmakers also weighed on the sector.

Hotter Inflation Raises Rate Hike Fears

The sell-off deepened after the Bureau of Labor Statistics on Wednesday reported that the U.S. Consumer Price Index (CPI) rose 3.7% year over year in September, up from 3.4% in August and above economists' expectations of 3.6%.

The reading raised concerns about further Federal Reserve interest-rate hikes, which could increase borrowing costs for companies financing large-scale AI infrastructure investments.

Applied Optoelectronics stock is at $88.99, down 9% in afternoon trading, though it remains up 155% year to date.

Meanwhile, Coherent Corp. (NYSE:COHR) stock is at $269.33, down 7% as it follows its smaller peer lower. Likewise, Lumentum Holdings (NASDAQ:LITE) stock is at $920.42, down 7% in step with Coherent. Such a tight range of losses points to a sector-wide revaluation of AI connectivity suppliers.
